meta.title: Who really said "The Only Time an Aircraft Has Too Much Fuel On Board Is When It Is On Fire"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Charles Kingsford Smith. The earliest known version is in Ernest K. Gann's 1974 Flying Circus. The Kingsford Smith credit first appears in a 2002 quote book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Only Time an Aircraft Has Too Much Fuel On Board Is When It Is On Fire'?
meta.ogDescription: An old pilots' adage, often pinned on Charles Kingsford Smith. Its earliest known form is in Ernest K. Gann's 1974 book; no evidence ties it to Smithy.

answer.label: Not Charles Kingsford Smith — earliest found in Ernest K. Gann
answer.sourceLine: The earliest version Quote Investigator located is in Gann’s 1974 book Ernest K. Gann’s Flying Circus: “the only time there was too much fuel aboard any aircraft was if it was on fire.” QI credits Gann “for now.” The polished popular wording, and the credit to Kingsford Smith, first appear in The Military Quotation Book (2002).

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: First printed, credited to Kingsford Smith, in James Charlton’s The Military Quotation Book (2002), p. 108

source.excerpt: …the only time there was too much fuel aboard any aircraft was if it was on fire.
trail: Quote Investigator says Gann’s 1974 book “contained the earliest appearance of the saying that QI has located.” Its conclusion: “QI would credit Ernest K. Gann for now” (Quote Investigator ↗).
By 1976 Shell Aviation News was treating the line as pilots’ lore: “Some domestic pilots contend that the only time too much fuel is aboard the aircraft is when it’s on fire” (Barry Popik ↗).

The exact popular wording appears, credited to Sir Charles Kingsford Smith, in James Charlton’s The Military Quotation Book (2002), p. 108. Popik finds no evidence that Kingsford Smith used the saying in his lifetime (Barry Popik ↗).
The Internet Archive has a catalog record for the 1974 Macmillan edition of Gann’s book (Internet Archive ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the fragment of Gann’s sentence as transcribed by Quote Investigator and Barry Popik. QI reports that chapter 22 is a revision of a 1968 Flying magazine article, and that the 1968 article does not contain the saying. The familiar wording, “The only time an aircraft has too much fuel on board is when it is on fire,” is a later rewording.

The popular wording is a later, unsigned rewording. Its first known printing is in a 2002 quotation book, and it has no identifiable author.

author.name: Ernest K. Gann
author.heading: About Ernest K. Gann
author.bio: Ernest Kellogg Gann was an American airline and wartime pilot. He became one of the best-known writers on flying, through the memoir Fate Is the Hunter (1961) and the novel The High and the Mighty (1953). His 1974 illustrated history Ernest K. Gann’s Flying Circus contains the earliest known form of this fuel maxim.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Smithy
misattribution.intro: The line circulates as an unsigned pilots’ adage. Quotation books have given it a famous aviator’s name. Kingsford Smith is a plausible choice, because his long-distance flights depended on fuel, but no record shows him saying it.

items.why: James Charlton’s The Military Quotation Book (2002) attributed the line to him. Quote Investigator found 1930 press coverage of his Atlantic attempt saying “There was not enough fuel,” but none of it contains the maxim. QI has no direct evidence that he said it (Quote Investigator ↗).

After Gann’s 1974 book, the saying spread as unattributed lore. Examples include Shell Aviation News (1976), a 1981 letter in Flying and a 1991 Richard L. Collins book that calls it “the old saw” (Barry Popik ↗).
Quote Investigator reports that a 1994 Washington Post article quoted an unnamed TWA captain with a version of the maxim (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest known printing is Ernest K. Gann’s, in his 1974 Flying Circus. Gann used the line without calling it an existing saying, and Quote Investigator credits him “for now,” pending earlier finds (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: A safety rule dressed as a joke
lead: The line is a pilot’s argument for loading as much fuel as possible. Extra weight costs something, but running out of fuel kills, and the only situation where fuel is purely a danger is a fire. That logic made it a natural fit for safety columns, training lore and lists of “rules of the air.” Along the way, the wording got smoothed into the version people quote today.

Kingsford Smith died in November 1935, when the Lady Southern Cross disappeared over the Andaman Sea (Wikipedia ↗). Every known printing of the saying, Gann’s first among them, comes from long after his death.
context.pull: Gann used it without calling it an old saying.
